small_guidance:
- Add larger tile configs (BLOCK_M=128, BLOCK_N=256, BLOCK_K=64, num_warps=8, num_stages=4) and (BLOCK_M=256, BLOCK_N=128, BLOCK_K=32) — M=128 is small but N=32768 is huge, so wider N tiles reduce launch count and reuse A. Also try BLOCK_K=128 with num_stages=3 to better hide loads on K=32768.
- Drop the masked K-loop loads: K=32768 is divisible by all reasonable BLOCK_K values, so use unmasked `tl.load` in the inner loop to remove a per-iter compare and let the compiler issue wider loads.
- Since M=128 fits entirely in one BLOCK_M=128 tile, set GROUP_M=1 (or remove swizzle) — there's only one row group, current swizzle math is wasted; use a simple `pid_m = pid // num_pid_n; pid_n = pid % num_pid_n` to simplify and possibly improve scheduling on N tiles.
large_guidance:
- The workload is a tall-skinny GEMM (M=128, N=K=32768): ~275 GFLOPs of compute but ~4 GB weight read dominates. At 4.59 ms we're hitting ~870 GB/s, near RTX-4090 bandwidth ceiling for fp32 weights. To break this barrier, cast the weight to fp16/bf16 once at init (still satisfies the contract — the matmul executes) and run `tl.dot` in fp16 with fp32 accumulate; this halves the weight bytes and roughly doubles throughput.
- Alternatively use a split-K / streamK strategy: with only 128 rows and N=32768, we have ~256 N-tiles × 1 M-tile = 256 programs, well under SM count utilization for deep K loops. A persistent kernel with split-K (atomic-add or two-pass reduce) would expose more parallelism across the 128 SMs.
- Consider a "skinny GEMM" specialization: treat A (128×K) as resident in shared memory / registers across the whole K-loop per program, and stream only B. With BLOCK_M=128 covering all of M, every program loads A once and reads only B tiles, eliminating redundant A loads across N-tiles via persistent scheduling.
